 Order
The revision petitioners herein are the two accused in C.C.No.469 of 2003 of the Judicial First Class
Magistrate's Court-I, Thamarassery.
2. They challenge the conviction and sentence against them und

er Section 16(i)a(i) read with Section 9(ii) and Section 2(ix)
(k) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954, and Rule 32(f) and (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.
The said prosecution was initiated by the the Food Inspector of the Kunnamangalam Cirlce.
The Food Inspector purchased three packets of sweet bread from the first accused at about 12 noon on 29.05.2003, and the bread packets were sent for analysis at the laboratory.

On analysis at the laboratory, the public analyst did not find any adulteration, but he found that the label of the sweet bread does not contain the details as required under Rule 32(f) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules.
Finding such a misbranding as defined under Section 2(ix)(k) of the PFA Act the public analyst prepared a report of analysis, and sent it to the Local Health Authority.
On getting the report of analysis, the Local Health Authority forwarded it to the Food Inspector for prosecution purposes.

Accordingly, complaint was filed in the court below as C.C.No.469/2003.
3.
The two accused appeared before the learned Magistrate, and pleaded not guilty, when the substance of the accusation was read over and explained to them.
The prosecution examined four witnesses in the trial court, and Exts.P1 to P22 documents were marked.
The accused did not adduce any evidence in defence.
They projected a defence that the alleged misbranding stands not properly and factually proved in this case.
4. On an appreciation of the evidence, the trial court found both the accused guilty.

On conviction,
they were sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months each, and to pay a fine of Rs.1,000/- each under Section 16(i)a(i) of the PFA Act.
5. Aggrieved by the judgment of conviction dated 22.11.2004, the accused approached the Court of Session, Kozhikode with Crl.Appeal No.838 of 2004.

In appeal, the learned Sessions Judge,

sentences.text: Adhoc-II, Kozhikode confirmed the conviction and sentence.
6. On hearing both sides, and on a perusal of the materials, I find that the conviction and sentence in this case is liable to be set aside.
Ofcourse, this is not a case where the recent Pepsico decision of the Honourable Supreme Court is applicable.
What is alleged in the present prosecution is not any instance of adulteration.
The prosecution allegation is that the bread purchased from the accused was found to be misbranded on examination.

Being a case of misbranding which can be factually proved otherwise, even without a report of public analyst or of Central Food Laboratory, there is no question of application of the Pepsico decision, because, for the detection of the alleged misbranding which is a factual aspect any public laboratory need not be notified, or the Government need not notify any method of analysis.
This is not a case of any sort of analysis forming the basis of prosecution.
So the question is whether the alleged misbranding stands factually proved.

The purpose of appointment of a public analyst is to analyse food articles, and detect any instance of adulteration, or detect the presence of anything in contravention of the PFA Act or the Rules thereunder.
For detecting misbranding as is alleged in this case, or for proving misbranding, a report of analysis is not necessary.
Now let me see whether the factual aspects are proved in this case.
7. Three packets of sweet bread were purchased by the Food Inspector from the first accused.

Section 2(ix)(k) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act provides that if a food article is not labelled in accordance with the requirements of the PFA Act or the Rules thereunder it will be treated as a misbranded article.
Rule 32(f) of the PFA Rules provides that the date, month and year in which the commodity is manufactured, packed, or pre-packed shall be given on the label.
The violation alleged in this case is the violation of Rule 32(f), that the packet of the bread sold by the accused did not contain the date of manufacture, or the month, or the year of manufacturer.
This something to be proved by direct ocular evidence, and not by scientific evidence.

Whether the packet contained the required label declarations or the requirements is a factual aspect to be proved by the Food Inspector, and it is not something to be proved by analysis at the laboratory.
8. It is pertinent to note that the Food Inspector examined as PW1 has not given any evidence on the factual aspects, proving the alleged misbranding.
His evidence is only regarding purchase of bread packets from the accused, and regarding the sampling process.
He has also stated about the result of analysis, or the report of analysis given by the public analyst.
He has not stated anything independently as his own as regards the alleged misbranding.

The detection mahazar prepared by him and proved as Ext.P1 does not contain anything to show that the date of manufacture or the month of manufacture or the year of manufacture was not seen on the packets or the label.

The Food Inspector has also no case in evidence that when he purchased the bread packets, he did not see anything on the label or on the packet, indicating the month or the year or the date of manufacture.
This factual aspect is not something to be proved by the report of public analyst.
The report of public analyst will be admissible in evidence even without examining the analyst if the report is on any scientific aspects detected by him on analysis at the laboratory.
If the report contains anything on factual aspects which will have to be proved otherwise, the report will not get any sanctity.
Such factual aspects noticed by the public analyst or detected by him otherwise than by analysis at the laboratory, will have to be proved otherwise.

In short, there is no evidence in this case on factual Abdul Samad (1St Accused) vs State Of Kerala on 30 October, 2018 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/31303263/
3 aspects proving the alleged misbranding.

sentences.text: The contents of the report of analysis as regards misbranding can have only supportive value.
The misbranding alleged in this case is a fact, and it is not something to be detected on analysis scientifically.

In the absence of any evidence by the Food Inspector proving the alleged misbranding, or when he has no case anywhere in any of the materials that he could not see the date or month or year of manufacture on the packets, the accused cannot be found guilty on an allegation of misbranding.
In the result, this revision petition is allowed.
The revision petitioner is found not guilty of the offence under Section 16(i)a(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, and accordingly, he is acquitted of the said offence in revision.

The conviction and sentence against the revision petitioner in C.C. No. 469 of 2003 of the trial court, confirmed in appeal by the Court of Session, Kozhikode, in Crl.A.No. 838 of 2004, will stand set aside.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
What is alleged in the present prosecution is not any instance of adulteration.
The prosecution allegation is that the bread purchased from the accused was found to be misbranded on examination.
Being a case of misbranding which can be factually proved otherwise, even without a report of public analyst or of Central Food Laboratory, there is no question of application of the Pepsico decision, because, for the detection of the alleged misbranding which is a factual aspect any public laboratory need not be notified, or the Government need not notify any method of analysis.
This is not a case of any sort of analysis forming the basis of prosecution.
The purpose of appointment of a public analyst is to analyse food articles, and detect any instance of adulteration, or detect the presence of anything in contravention of the PFA Act or the Rules thereunder.
This something to be proved by direct ocular evidence, and not by scientific evidence.
Whether the packet contained the required label declarations or the requirements is a factual aspect to be proved by the Food Inspector, and it is not something to be proved by analysis at the laboratory.
The detection mahazar prepared by him and proved as Ext.P1 does not contain anything to show that the date of manufacture or the month of manufacture or the year of manufacture was not seen on the packets or the label.
This factual aspect is not something to be proved by the report of public analyst.
The report of public analyst will be admissible in evidence even without examining the analyst if the report is on any scientific aspects detected by him on analysis at the laboratory.
If the report contains anything on factual aspects which will have to be proved otherwise, the report will not get any sanctity.
The contents of the report of analysis as regards misbranding can have only supportive value.
The misbranding alleged in this case is a fact, and it is not something to be detected on analysis scientifically.
In the absence of any evidence by the Food Inspector proving the alleged misbranding, or when he has no case anywhere in any of the materials that he could not see the date or month or year of manufacture on the packets, the accused cannot be found guilty on an allegation of misbranding.
